questiontext.text:
In Step 2 of the proof above we assume that the statement holds for \(n = k\). A student objects: ‘That is assuming what we are trying to prove.’

Which of these statements are correct? Select all that apply.

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 3 proves an implication: for every positive integer \(k\), if the statement holds for \(n = k\), then it holds for \(n = k+1\). To prove ‘if A then B’ you assume A and deduce B. So Step 2 assumes the statement for one value, \(n = k\), as the ‘if’ part of that implication. This is the induction hypothesis. Nothing is assumed about every \(n\), so the proof is not circular.

The assumption is not deduced from Step 1 either. Step 1 gives only \(n = 1\). The value of \(k\) is arbitrary, so the argument in Step 3 must work whichever positive integer \(k\) is.

Think of the dominoes: Step 3 shows that each domino knocks over the next one, and Step 1 pushes the first one. Neither step on its own knocks them all down; together they do.

The correct statements are the second and the fourth.

questionvariables.text: ta1: [[e_alln, false, "Step 2 assumes that the statement holds for every positive integer \\(n\\)."], [e_impl, true, "Step 2 assumes the statement for one value, \\(n = k\\), in order to prove that if it holds for \\(n = k\\) then it holds for \\(n = k+1\\)."], [e_fromone, false, "Step 2 is justified because Step 1 showed that the statement holds for \\(n = 1\\), so it holds for \\(n = k\\)."], [e_arb, true, "The value of \\(k\\) is arbitrary, so the argument in Step 3 has to work whichever positive integer \\(k\\) is."]];

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 7.1 (Step 2 of Solution 7.1-B, pp. 28-29) in Section 7 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Correct. Step 3 proves an implication for an arbitrary \(k\), and to prove ‘if A then B’ you assume A. Nothing is assumed about every \(n\).
Assuming the statement for every \(n\) would indeed be circular, but Step 2 does not do that. Read Step 2 again: for how many values of \(n\) is the statement assumed?
Step 1 gives only \(n = 1\), and nothing follows from it about \(n = k\). The assumption in Step 2 is not deduced from anything that came before.

falsefeedback.text: Nothing you have chosen is wrong, but more than one of the statements is correct. Think about what Step 3 has to prove, and for which values of \(k\).

qtest.description: The circular reading added to the two correct
Only one of the two correct statements
